dataset.name: Greenhouse Rhizobox Experiment with Plant Characteristics, Porewater, Gas Flux, and Soil Biogeochemistry data, Seward Peninsula, Alaska, 2024
description: Data collected from a greenhouse rhizobox experiment (2024) using soils and plants collected at Council, AK (64°51’35.0”N 163°41’59.1”W) during a summer campaign in 2023. Water data consists of soil porewater collected by porewater samplers (rhizons). Gas data consists of CO2 and CH4 surface soil fluxes measured with an FTIR (Fourier-transformed infrared red) analyzer. Plant and root data consists of biomass, root length. This study is a part of The Next-Generation Ecosystem Experiments: Arctic (NGEE Arctic), was a research effort to reduce uncertainty in Earth System Models by developing a predictive understanding of carbon-rich Arctic ecosystems and feedbacks to climate. NGEE Arctic was supported by the Department of Energy's Office of Biological and Environmental Research.

The NGEE Arctic project had two field research sites: 1) located within the Arctic polygonal tundra coastal region on the Barrow Environmental Observatory (BEO) and the North Slope near Utqiagvik (Barrow), Alaska and 2) multiple areas on the discontinuous permafrost region of the Seward Peninsula north of Nome, Alaska. Through observations, experiments, and synthesis with existing datasets, NGEE Arctic provided an enhanced knowledge base for multi-scale modeling and contributed to improved process representation at global pan-Arctic scales within the Department of Energy's Earth system Model (the Energy Exascale Earth System Model, or E3SM), and specifically within the E3SM Land Model component (ELM).

This dataset was generated to broadly address the following research question: how will climate change (i.e., thawing permafrost, landscape change) alter the ecosystem flux (sink versus source) of important greenhouse gases such as CO2 and CH4?
Description of the contents of this data package:
Rhizobox2024_Data.csv: This dataset contains plant, water and gas data. No software is needed to utilize them.

spatialCoverage.description: The field campaign was conducted from August 30th to September 4th 2023 near Council, AK (64°51’35.0”N 163°41’59.1”W) (Figure 1) as part of the Next Generation Ecosystem Experiment in the Arctic (NGEE Arctic) project (https://ngee-arctic.ornl.gov/). This continental site was characterized as a discontinuous permafrost region with lowland thermokarst wetlands and adjacent upland tussock tundra (Figure 1). Vegetation in the lowland thermokarst wetlands was primarily colonized by aerenchymous graminoids while the upland tundra consisted of a moist acidic tussock tundra community containing a heterogeneous mixture of bryophyte, lichen, graminoids, forbs, and dwarf deciduous and evergreen shrubs (Yang et al. 2021). Our sampling scheme was designed to pair soil, plant, porewater, and GHG flux measurements across these two adjacent landscape positions, as well as across differing PFTs within the upland tussock community (the lowland thermokarst wetland was dominated by only one PFT). We collected data from eight total plots: four in lowland thermokarst wetlands and four in adjacent upland tussock tundra (Figure 1), hereafter referred to as lowland and upland. Within each selected location, a 1-m × 1-m plot with nine 33-cm × 33-cm subplots were designated for plant, soil, porewater, and GHG flux sampling.

measurementTechnique:
2.0 Methods
2.1 Field Site and Soil and Plant Collection
Our field site is in a discontinuous permafrost region near Council, AK, USA, (Yoshikawa and Hinzman 2003) and is part of the Next Generation Ecosystem Experiment-Arctic (NGEE-Arctic) project. We collected soils for this experiment in a saturated thermokarst wetland containing the aerenchymas graminoid, Eriophorum vaginatum. Intact blocks of soil containing Eriophorum (~0-30cm depth) were removed using a long-serrated metal knife. Each block of soil and intact plants were placed into plastic bags on ice and transported back to Oak Ridge National Laboratory in coolers. Surface water collected from the thermokarst wetland was transported back to the lab in 1 L Nalgene bottles on ice, and frozen for shipment. Upon arrival to the lab, Eriophorum plants were separated into smaller plugs (~2 cm diameter). These were placed in soil from the field site and lived in a greenhouse for approximately 3 months before they were transplanted into rhizoboxes.
2.2 Rhizobox Construction and Setup
Here we used the rhizobox approach which has previously been identified as a strong method for connecting above and belowground plant-soil interactions (Neumann et al. 2009; Luo et al. 2018). Twenty custom-made rhizoboxes were constructed of transparent acrylic measuring 11cm x 3cm x 30cm (LxWxH; Figure 1). Each rhizobox was outfitted with three porewater rhizon samplers with a pore size of 0.20μm (Rhizosphere Research Products, Model 1908) inserted horizontally at 5cm, 15cm and 25cm depth below the soil surface. Homogenized soil collected from the lowland thermokarst wetland was rewetted using surface water collected from the thermokarst wetland and the soil was placed into the rhizoboxes. Eriophorum plugs were then carefully transplanted into ten of the rhizoboxes while the other ten rhizoboxes were soil only. The two treatments are hereafter referred to as “plant-soil” and “soil-only”. All twenty rhizoboxes were then fully flooded to the soil surface using surface water collected at the thermokarst wetland. Approximately 50mL of the field-collected surface water was added to all 20 boxes once a week to keep the soil fully saturated despite losses to surface evaporation, evapotranspiration, and small leaks (<10mL/week). Rhizoboxes were kept on a rack that maintained them at a 30° angle to encourage root growth towards one side of the boxes for root imaging (later described in detail). When not being imaged, rhizoboxes were covered with non-transparent foil sheeting to minimize root exposure to light and reduce belowground algal
growth. All rhizoboxes were maintained in a greenhouse for the duration of the experiment with controlled light 15 hours per day at 500 μmol photons m-2 s-1 (±100) and temperature conditions of 24ºC (±4).
Figure 1. Image of the rhizoboxes used for this experiment. The boxes sat on a rack at a 30º angle so that imaging would capture a greater degree of downward root growth. Rhizon porewater samplers were installed at three different depths below the soil surface. Racks consist of five rhizoboxes. Two racks were plant-soil (depicted here) and two racks were soil-only (n=10). Transparent sides were covered with non-transparent foil when not being imaged.
2.3 Porewater Collection and Analysis
Porewater was collected every other week from the three rhizon samplers in each of the twenty rhizoboxes using a 25mL luer lock vacuum syringe. Once enough porewater collected in the syringe (~6mL), an aliquot was immediately measured using calibrated probes for pH, DO (Mettler Toledo) and redox (Extech RE 300). The remaining porewater was preserved for later analysis using the following procedures. Approximately 2mL of sample was placed inside combusted glass amber vials with concentrated HCl for DOC analysis (Shimadzu, TOC-L) and for Fe2+ assessment using the 1,10 phenanthroline method (HACH Method 8008).
Approximately 1mL of sample was placed inside glass amber vials with HNO3 for total elements analysis (Fe, P, Ca, Si, Mg, K, Mn) (Aligent, ICP-OES), with analytical blanks being below the detection limit. Approximately 1mL of sample was placed inside glass amber vials and used for excitation-emission-matrices (EEMs) ultra-violet-visible (UV-VIS) analysis (Horiba, Aqualog). The Aqualog was calibrated using deionized water blanks and data were normalized to the instrument’s Raman Area. Wavelengths between 230 and 700 nm were measured with a measurement step of 2 nm. Fluorescence peak intensities (i.e., Coble Peaks normalized by DOC concentration) and indices (FI, HIX, BIX) were determined, as well as absorbance indices (i.e., ABS254, Sr, SUVA254, E2:E3). These peaks and indices were calculated using previously established equations (Ohno 2002; Weishaar et al. 2003; Baker et al. 2008; Helms et al. 2008; Huguet et al. 2009; Cory et al. 2010).
2.4 Trace Plant-Soil Gas Fluxes
Plant-soil gas fluxes (CO2, CH4) were measured weekly. We also measured N2O and NH3, but the flux slopes were near zero, so we did not include those gases in the final dataset. We used a closed-chamber approach in which a gas impermeable chamber constructed of polyethylene was gently placed onto the top of each rhizobox and screwed shut with vacuum grease to create an airtight seal. A small fan was inside the chamber during measurements and ensured an evenly mixed headspace. The flux chamber was connected to a portable Fourier transformed infrared (FTIR) gas analyzer (Picarro G2508) outfitted with gas impermeable tubing that was routed through a 16-port distribution manifold to allow consecutive, automated measurements of the rhizoboxes. Light and temperature conditions present during fluxes were monitored with a pendant sensor (HOBO, Onset). Four LED strips were placed directly above the rhizoboxes during measurement to ensure consistent and abundant light conditions during weekly flux measurements with a Photosynthetic Photon Flux Density (PPFD) of 200 μmol m-2 s-1. Gas fluxes (μmol m-2 s-1) were calculated by monitoring changes in gas concentration inside the enclosed rhizoboxes every 1s. Each chamber was monitored for 5 minutes in total, but the first two minutes were discarded as the gas circulation stabilized inside the chamber. The final 3 minutes of each measurement were used to determine the slope (i.e., ppm s-1). A linear fit was applied to calculate Δc/Δt using Excel. For all fluxes, positive values indicate a net flux of a gas out of the plant-soil or soil-only system into the headspace atmosphere, while a negative value indicates a net flux of a gas out of the atmosphere into the plant-soil or soil-only system. The R2 values for all CO2 and CH4 fluxes (n = 265) were considered good linear fits (R2 > 0.80), indicating stable conditions during measurements (Petrakis et al. 2017; Barba et al. 2019; Capooci and Vargas 2022; Fettrow et al. 2023b, a). We decided to omit the first three weeks of gas flux measurements, as we believe the gas fluctuations were still equilibrating during this time. In the plant-soil treatments, gross primary productivity (GPP) was calculated by taking gas fluxes with the lights on and subtracting from fluxes taken with the lights off. We refer to the dark measurements as ecosystem respiration (Reco) as these measurements represent respiration from both the plants and soil. Net ecosystem exchange (NEE) describes the net uptake (sink) or emission (source) of CO2 based on GPP in the plants and Reco in the plants and soil. NEE is calculated for plant-soil treatments only, since soil-only treatments did not have plants.
2.4 Root Imaging
In-situ root images were taken weekly in the plant-soil treatments. This was done using a USB controlled camera (Basler, A5472) connected to RhizoVisionImager (Seethepalli et al. 2021). Rhizoboxes were placed in a small photo booth enclosure to ensure consistent lighting conditions. We labeled the camera position and rhizobox positions so that every week the images were taken in the same spatial orientation. Root images were analyzed in RhizoVisionExplorer (Seethepalli et al. 2021) to extract visible root length using the same parameters across all images. Images were analyzed by depth intervals corresponding to the depths around the three rhizon samplers (0-10cm, 10cm-20cm, 20cm-30cm). An example of root tracing in RhizoVision can be found in Supplemental Information (Figure S1).
2.5 Post Experiment Destructive Plant and Root Sampling
After the end of the experiment, aboveground and belowground plant parts were destructively harvested from the plant-soil rhizoboxes. All leaves, sheaths, and rhizomes were removed. These tissues were immediately dried in an oven (70 °C) for 72 hours and weighed. In
addition, soil from each rhizobox was sectioned into three depth intervals (0-10cm, 10cm-20cm, 20cm-30cm), corresponding with the rhizon sampler locations. Fine roots in the soil were identified as transport roots or absorptive roots (McCormack et al. 2015). Transport roots and absorptive roots were independently scanned at high resolution (1400dpi) on a flatbed scanner, and WinRhizo was used to measure total root length and average diameter. Fine roots were then dried in the oven and weighed so that specific root length (SRL ;m g-1) and the fine root contribution to belowground biomass could be calculated.
